patient.name: Victor Ashworth
patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral leg numbness and weakness over 2 years, labeled CIDP but not responding to IVIG
patient.hpi: Victor Ashworth is a 61-year-old retired marine engineer presenting for a second opinion after 2 years of progressive bilateral leg numbness and weakness that has been diagnosed as CIDP at an outside institution. He received 6 courses of IVIG (2 g/kg) over 18 months with minimal sustained benefit — each course provides 2-3 weeks of modest improvement followed by return to baseline. His neurologist at the outside institution has recommended switching to rituximab. Victor is seeking a second opinion before proceeding. He has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) which was noted incidentally at his CIDP workup, and his outside neurologist acknowledged it could be contributing. He notes that his symptoms began with bilateral foot burning and numbness (which he still attributes to the 'neuropathy') and progressed to leg weakness. He has been unable to walk more than 2 blocks. He reports occasional diarrhea (3-4x/week, watery, several months) which he attributes to diabetes or metformin. He has unintentionally lost 9 kg over 18 months, attributed to 'watching his diet' for diabetes. He notes that his skin has changed in the past year — skin darkening (hyperpigmentation) on his face and hands, and his hair has become unusually coarse. He also reports that his ankles have been swelling despite normal cardiac echo at his outside institution. He provided outside records showing: NCS with moderately demyelinating features, CSF protein 62 mg/dL, outside neurologist's diagnosis: 'probable CIDP, IVIG-refractory.'
patient.review_of_systems: Positive: bilateral leg numbness and weakness, bilateral ankle edema, unintentional 9 kg weight loss, skin hyperpigmentation (face and hands), coarse hair changes, diarrhea (3-4x/week, watery, several months). Negative: fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, dyspnea, cognitive changes, bowel blood.

report.summary: NCS/EMG REVIEW (repeat in-house, comparison with prior outside study). DEMYELINATING SENSORIMOTOR POLYNEUROPATHY — consistent with POEMS syndrome neuropathy. Pattern differs subtly from CIDP: POEMS neuropathy typically has more severe axonal loss SUPERIMPOSED on demyelination, and the CSF protein elevation is often dramatic. Outside NCS interpretation as 'CIDP' was not technically wrong but missed the systemic POEMS context.

motor.flag: markedly prolonged DML, low amplitude, slow velocity — demyelinating + axonal

emg.summary: Mixed demyelinating and axonal pattern. Demyelination with secondary axonal loss — consistent with POEMS syndrome neuropathy. This NCS pattern in isolation could be called 'CIDP-like' but the systemic features (papilledema, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, skin changes, M-protein, elevated VEGF) clearly indicate POEMS.

report.overall_impression: POEMS SYNDROME NEUROPATHY — not CIDP. The NCS is 'CIDP-like' (demyelinating) but the clinical and laboratory context is POEMS. TREATMENT: POEMS requires treatment of the underlying plasma cell dyscrasia. For localized osteosclerotic plasmacytoma: radiation therapy. For systemic disease: autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT). IVIG is ineffective in POEMS. VEGF inhibitors (bevacizumab) have shown efficacy. Anti-VEGF mechanism: lenalidomide + dexamethasone reduce VEGF. Endocrine replacement therapy required for hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, adrenal insufficiency.

report.summary: Bone marrow biopsy: IgA lambda plasma cells 8% of cellularity — borderline MGUS vs myeloma. Osteosclerotic changes NOT evident in iliac crest sample. Immunohistochemistry: lambda-restricted plasma cells. No Castleman disease features.
report.interpretation: 8% lambda plasma cells — borderline MGUS vs myeloma (myeloma threshold is plasma cells >10% or myeloma-defining event). Given POEMS diagnosis, systemic chemotherapy is indicated even for borderline plasma cell burden. Referral to hematology for ASCT evaluation. Whole-body PET-CT or skeletal survey for osteosclerotic lesions — osteosclerotic myeloma (sclerotic plasmacytomas) is the plasma cell dyscrasia most commonly associated with POEMS.

report.summary: FDG-PET/CT: Single osteosclerotic lesion in T8 vertebra (SUV 3.2, sclerotic morphology on CT — low FDG uptake, consistent with osteosclerotic myeloma). No lytic lesions. No additional plasmacytomas. No Castleman disease adenopathy pattern. ASSESSMENT: SOLITARY OSTEOSCLEROTIC PLASMACYTOMA at T8.
report.clinical_significance: SOLITARY OSTEOSCLEROTIC PLASMACYTOMA is the most common plasma cell dyscrasia in POEMS. TREATMENT: Radiation therapy to T8 plasmacytoma (50 Gy in 28 fractions) — definitive treatment for solitary POEMS plasmacytoma. Expected VEGF reduction after radiation: begins at 3-6 months. Neuropathy improvement: 50-70% partial recovery over 12-24 months post-radiation. ASCT considered for multifocal or systemic POEMS.

report.summary: Fundoscopy: bilateral optic disc elevation with blurred margins (grade 1 papilledema). OCT (optical coherence tomography): retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickening bilaterally — peripapillary RNFL elevated right 168 mcm (normal <120 mcm), left 152 mcm. Visual acuity: 20/25 bilaterally. No hemorrhages, no exudates. Visual fields: bilateral enlarged blind spots (consistent with papilledema). Humphrey visual field test: bilateral enlargement of physiological blind spot only, no arcuate or central scotoma.
report.interpretation: PAPILLEDEMA confirmed bilateral (grade 1). In POEMS syndrome, papilledema is caused by VEGF-mediated CNS vascular permeability and intracranial hypertension. MRI brain/MRV needed to confirm elevated ICP and exclude venous sinus thrombosis. Visual acuity preserved currently but bilateral papilledema requires treatment to prevent visual loss. POEMS treatment (radiation) will reduce VEGF and resolve papilledema.

POEMS Treatment Response (4 months post-.value: Foot drop improving: dorsiflexion 4/5 bilateral (from 3/5). Walking 4 blocks (from 2 blocks). Pain improved to 4/10 from 7/10.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: POEMS syndrome (Polyneuropathy, Organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, M-protein, Skin changes) from solitary osteosclerotic plasmacytoma at T8
critical_actions: Recognize IVIG failure (6 courses) as a CIDP misdiagnosis flag — true CIDP responds to IVIG
Fundoscopy with direct examination — bilateral papilledema is present on examination; this is NOT a CIDP feature
Order VEGF level — the key biomarker for POEMS diagnosis (markedly elevated in POEMS)
Order SPEP — IgA lambda paraprotein is the M-protein criterion for POEMS
Multi-organ systemic evaluation: endocrine (all axes), skin (hyperpigmentation), ophthalmology (papilledema), edema
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT give further IVIG — POEMS is IVIG-refractory; each IVIG course wastes resources and delays correct diagnosis
Do NOT start rituximab for presumed CIDP — rituximab targets B cells; POEMS requires plasma cell-directed therapy
Do NOT miss the ophthalmological examination — bilateral papilledema is present and was present throughout the illness; fundoscopy should be part of every neuropathy examination
Do not treat endocrine abnormalities as independent coincidental findings — in POEMS, all endocrine dysfunction is from the same VEGF-mediated mechanism

differential.key_distinguishing: CIDP responds to IVIG — POEMS does not; CIDP does not cause papilledema, endocrinopathy, skin changes, or markedly elevated VEGF; M-protein 1.8 g/dL and VEGF elevation are not CIDP features; 6 IVIG courses with minimal benefit should prompt reconsideration
Diabetes HbA1c 8.2% cannot explain papilledema, multiple endocrine abnormalities, M-protein, VEGF 1840, and skin changes; IVIG failure with all these systemic features demands POEMS evaluation

Myeloma typically causes lytic lesions and hypercalcemia (neither present here); osteosclerotic plasmacytoma is specific to POEMS; VEGF elevation is characteristic of POEMS not myeloma; bone marrow plasma cells borderline (8%, threshold for myeloma is >10%)

key_reasoning_points: DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE: CIDP-like NCS pattern created anchoring; 6 IVIG courses given based on incorrect diagnosis; systematic failure to perform fundoscopy and skin/edema examination perpetuated the error
KEY PRINCIPLE: ANY patient with 'CIDP' not responding to IVIG after 2-3 courses should have POEMS workup (SPEP, VEGF, complete physical exam including fundoscopy)
IVIG FAILURE: True CIDP responds to IVIG in 70-80% of patients; 6 courses with minimal sustained benefit is a definitive red flag
PAPILLEDEMA DIAGNOSTIC CLUE: Bilateral papilledema is NOT seen in CIDP; it should immediately prompt POEMS, intracranial hypertension, or CSF obstruction workup

VEGF ELEVATION: Serum VEGF >600 pg/mL is a major diagnostic criterion for POEMS and the pathogenic mediator of all manifestations; ordering VEGF should be reflexive in any 'CIDP-like' neuropathy with M-protein

OSTEOSCLEROTIC MYELOMA: The plasma cell dyscrasia in POEMS is osteosclerotic (not lytic) — standard myeloma workup looking for lytic lesions will be normal; PET-CT is needed to detect sclerotic lesions
TREATMENT DIFFERENCE: Solitary POEMS plasmacytoma — radiation therapy is curative in 50-70%; systemic POEMS — ASCT; neither responds to IVIG
